_readme: CONNECTICUT CIVIL DEADLINE RULES -- 1 row, Practice Book Sec. 10-8.
== DO NOT ADD A CONNECTICUT CALENDAR ==================================
DO NOT ADD A CONNECTICUT CALENDAR UNTIL THE FIRST-DAY-CONVENTION
SOURCING QUESTION IS ANSWERED -- DOING SO WOULD SILENTLY COMPUTE LATE.
The question, in one sentence: DOES PRACTICE BOOK SEC. 63-2 REACH
SUPERIOR COURT PLEADINGS, OR ONLY APPEALS? Sec. 63-2 is the sole source
for `the last day shall, and the first day shall not, be counted`, and it
sits under RULES OF APPELLATE PROCEDURE. If it does not reach trial-court
filings, the first-day convention this seed counts on is ASSUMED RATHER
THAN SOURCED, and a wrong assumption there moves every Connecticut date
ONE DAY LATE -- the direction that loses a filing. Full working at
docs/sairnlaw-connecticut-deadline-seed-gate.md Sec. 3a.
This is a SEPARATE blocker from the Wisconsin hazard below, and it is the
more dangerous of the two because it fails LATE where every other
disclosed Connecticut gap fails EARLY. BOTH must be answered before a
`ct` calendar is loaded -- resolving only the closure schedule is not
enough. Confirmed as a hard block on Michael's direction 2026-08-27.
The absent calendar is what currently enforces this. Do not treat that as
an oversight to tidy up: `api/_lib/deadline-connecticut.test.js` fails on
purpose if a `ct` calendar appears, and that failure is the reminder to
come back and read this paragraph.
== READ THIS FIRST: THIS FILE DOES NOT PRODUCE DATES =================
Connecticut is the FIRST jurisdiction seeded with NO holiday calendar,
and that is deliberate. rollOff() consults the calendar BEFORE it looks
at the weekday, so with no `ct` calendar loaded every computation returns
NOT_PROVISIONED -- on every date, not just on weekends. Loading this file
gives the engine a rule it can FIND and REFUSE, which is the point: a
caller asking for a Connecticut deadline is told Connecticut is not
provisioned instead of being told nothing exists. The refusal IS the hold
on the rollover basis (see THE WISCONSIN HAZARD below). It is enforced by
the absent calendar, not by anyone remembering to leave it out.
Verified 2026-08-27 against the engine as written, not assumed.
== SOURCE -- among the cleanest of any state gated =====================
The Judicial Branch publishes the OFFICIAL 2026 CONNECTICUT PRACTICE BOOK
as one free PDF on a plain curl: jud.ct.gov/Publications/PracticeBook/PB.pdf
-- HTTP 200, 3,702,299 bytes, 699 pages, re-fetched and re-extracted
2026-08-27. It is real text, not a scan. Page 1 reads OFFICIAL / 2026 /
CONNECTICUT PRACTICE BOOK / (Revision of 1998), and every section carries
its own dated amendment line, so effective_from is a REAL per-rule date
here rather than a restyling fallback (contrast Minnesota Rules 33/34/36).
Sec. 10-8's line reads: (Amended June 14, 2013, to take effect Jan. 1,
2014.) -- hence effective_from 2014-01-01. cga.ct.gov serves the General
Statutes free on plain curl as well. Nothing here is a source problem.
== THE SHAPE: A CHAIN, NOT A DEADLINE FROM A TRIGGER ==================
Sec. 10-8 is a rolling cadence. The first step runs thirty days from the
RETURN DAY; every step after that runs thirty days from THE PRECEDING
PLEADING, or from the filing of the court's decision on it where one was
required -- so the nth deadline depends on the (n-1)th ACTUAL FILING DATE,
indefinitely. Every other seeded jurisdiction computes ONE date from ONE
caller-supplied trigger. Maryland's chained discovery floor was logged as
the highest-stakes shape found in any gate because ONE LIMB depended on
another rule's output; Connecticut's entire pleading cadence is that shape
as its PRIMARY mechanism, and it chains without limit.
That is modellable only in one honest form, which is what this row is: a
caller who supplies the date of the preceding pleading gets a correct
thirty-day answer. Hence trigger_event `filing_of_preceding_pleading` --
named at length precisely so nobody reads it as `return_day`.
CONNECTICUT HAS NO SINGLE ANSWER DEADLINE TO COMPUTE. There is no `answer
due` row in this file and there must not be one. Any UI surfacing this
jurisdiction has to say so in words, not imply a date exists.
== WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT SEEDED ====================================
(1) THE FIRST STEP -- thirty days from the RETURN DAY. The return day is a
Connecticut-specific date STATED IN THE WRIT and fixed by Conn. Gen. Stat.
Sec. 52-48, which has not been read. It is NOT derivable from a service
date and a seed must never silently equate the two. Seeding this needs the
statute read and a caller-supplied `return_day` input.
(2) THE TWO DOMAIN VARIANTS riding on the same sentence -- SUMMARY PROCESS
= THREE days, MORTGAGE FORECLOSURE = FIFTEEN days. Both are real and both
are quoted in the authority note below. They are held back only because
they need a domain decision (this engine's DOMAIN_LABELS knows
civil-litigation and appellate; neither names summary process or
foreclosure), not because of any doubt about the text. The three-day
period is short enough that an intermediate-day rule would matter -- and
Connecticut has none, affirmatively, so the arithmetic is not the risk.
(3) Discovery rows. Secs. 13-6, 13-9, 13-22 and 13-23 were located but not
read. (4) Appellate rows. (5) Any backward row -- no backward provision
was found, so rollover_suffix_backward on ct_pb_63_2 is blank.
== THE COUNTING RULE IS IN THE APPELLATE CHAPTER (LATE-DIRECTION RISK) ==
NEW ON 2026-08-27, not in the gate document. Sec. 63-2 supplies the whole
counting rule -- last day counted, first day not, calendar not working
days -- and it sits under RULES OF APPELLATE PROCEDURE. It is nonetheless
the ONLY day-counting provision in the book: `first day shall` occurs
EXACTLY ONCE in 699 pages, there, and searches for `computation of time`,
`computing any period`, `period of time prescribed` and `intermediate
Saturdays` return ZERO hits each. There is no trial-court equivalent.
Two textual points argue 63-2 still reaches a Superior Court filing: it
governs `any documents ... under these rules or an order of the court`,
and its own rollover sentence expressly names `the office of the clerk of
the TRIAL COURT or of the appellate clerk`. Neither is conclusive.
IF 63-2 DOES NOT REACH TRIAL-COURT PLEADINGS, the first-day/last-day
convention applied here is ASSUMED RATHER THAN SOURCED, and a wrong
assumption on that point computes LATE -- the direction that loses a
filing. This is the one thing in this file that fails in the unsafe
direction, and it is tolerable ONLY because nothing computes at all.
RESOLVE IT BEFORE ANY `ct` CALENDAR IS LOADED.
== THE WISCONSIN HAZARD: THE ROLLOVER HAS NO HOLIDAY BASIS ============
Running the standing weekend-coverage check -- if the rule does not name
Saturday and Sunday, does a holiday statute cover both, everywhere? --
Connecticut FAILS THE PREMISE: there is no holiday list in play at all.
`Holiday` appears FIVE times in the entire Practice Book and not once as a
definition or a computation rule. Both rollover tests key on ONE thing:
THE CLERK'S OFFICE IS CLOSED. Sec. 7-17: `If the last day for filing any
matter in the clerk's office falls on a day on which such office is not
open ... then the last day for filing shall be the next business day upon
which such office is open.`
So weekends come out right only BY ACCIDENT OF FACT -- offices are shut
Saturdays and Sundays -- while the BASIS is closure. Encoding Conn. Gen.
Stat. Sec. 1-4's statutory holiday list as the `ct` calendar would be WRONG
IN THE LATE DIRECTION on any listed day a clerk's office is in fact open.
Sec. 7-17 says offices close `during weeks which include a legal holiday`
and NEVER SAYS WHICH DAYS THOSE ARE. That is precisely what left Wisconsin
gated. The operative artifact is the JUDICIAL BRANCH'S OWN PUBLISHED
COURT-CLOSURE SCHEDULE, making Connecticut ingest-not-derive like NC, NJ,
MD and OK. DO NOT BUILD A `ct` CALENDAR FROM THE STATUTORY LIST.
== NO SERVICE EXTENSION -- NOW AFFIRMATIVE, NOT MERELY ABSENT ==========
The gate reported this as a searched-for absence. It is stronger than that.
Re-run 2026-08-27 on DE-HYPHENATED, whitespace-flattened text (the gate's
search ran on raw extraction, where `calen-\ndar` could have hidden hits;
it did not): `days shall be added`, `shall be added to the prescribed`,
`additional time after service`, `three days shall be added`, `additional
(three|five) days` -- ZERO hits each. No added-days provision exists.
And Sec. 10-13 states the positive rule: `SERVICE BY MAIL IS COMPLETE UPON
MAILING.` So Connecticut does not extend for mail; it completes on mailing.
Every other seeded jurisdiction has an added-days provision -- Connecticut
genuinely has none. NOT DISPOSITIVE: the General Statutes were still not
searched for an equivalent, and `no extension` is exactly the assumption
that computes EARLY on every mailed period if wrong. Safe direction, still
worth closing.
IRRELEVANT TO THIS ROW EITHER WAY: this rule runs from the FILING of the
preceding pleading, not from service of anything. No service_extension and
no service_completion block is carried, and adding one would be a field the
engine reads for a trigger that is not a service event.
== TWO EARLY-DIRECTION LIMBS, RECORDED, NOT MODELLED ==================
(1) Sec. 7-17's DISCRETIONARY closure -- `closed pursuant to authorization
by the administrative judge in consultation with the chief court
administrator ... due to the existence of special circumstances`. Not
knowable in advance.
(2) NEW ON 2026-08-27, not in the gate document: Sec. 7-17's E-FILING
OUTAGE limb -- if the court's electronic filing system is nonoperational
for thirty consecutive minutes between 9 a.m. and 3 p.m., or for ANY period
between 3 and 5 p.m., on the last day, a document received the next
business day is timely. Also not knowable in advance.
Both can only ever make a real deadline LATER than this engine's date, so
omitting them reports EARLY. Filing early is safe.
== AN E-FILING CUTOFF THAT MOVES THE FILING, NOT THE DEADLINE ==========
Sec. 7-17 also deems a document e-received after 5 p.m. on an open day, or
at any time on a closed day, filed on the next business day. Mechanically
Missouri's service-completion shape applied to FILING rather than service.
It does not change the date this engine would report; it means a filer has
until 5 p.m. on that date rather than midnight. Recorded in the row note,
not modelled as a mechanism.
== NO JURISDICTION_COVERAGE ENTRY, ON PURPOSE =========================
That table's text rides on SUCCESSFUL computations. Connecticut never
produces one, so a `ct` entry would be dormant code that no caller can
reach -- a Guardian 0d violation. Add it in the SAME change that adds the
calendar, never before.
== BEFORE ANY `ct` CALENDAR IS LOADED, RESOLVE ========================
(a) HARD BLOCK, LATE DIRECTION -- whether Sec. 63-2's counting reaches
trial-court filings. See the DO NOT ADD A CONNECTICUT CALENDAR block
at the top of this readme. Answering (b) without answering (a) does
NOT unblock the calendar.
(b) HARD BLOCK, LATE DIRECTION -- the Judicial Branch court-closure
schedule as the calendar's basis, NOT Conn. Gen. Stat. Sec. 1-4.
(c) Conn. Gen. Stat. Sec. 52-48 -- how the return day is fixed.
(d) Whether the General Statutes carry a service extension.
(a) AND (b) BOTH block the calendar, independently, and both fail LATE.
(c) blocks the return-day row only. (d) blocks nothing seeded here.

rules.label: Advance the pleadings one step after the preceding pleading (Connecticut) — NOT an answer deadline

authority.quote: Commencing on the return day of the writ, summons and complaint in civil actions, pleadings, including motions and requests addressed to the pleadings, shall advance within thirty days from the return day, and any subsequent pleadings, motions and requests shall advance at least one step within each successive period of thirty days from the preceding pleading or the filing of the decision of the judicial authority thereon if one is required, except that in summary process actions the time period shall be three days and in actions to foreclose a mortgage on real estate the time period shall be fifteen days. The filing of interrogatories or requests for discovery shall not suspend the time requirements of this section unless upon motion of either party the judicial authority shall find that there is good cause to suspend such time requirements.
authority.note: THIS IS NOT AN ANSWER DEADLINE AND CONNECTICUT HAS NONE TO COMPUTE. Sec. 10-8 is a self-perpetuating CHAIN, not a period from a fixed trigger: each step runs thirty days from THE PRECEDING PLEADING (or from the filing of the court's decision on it, where one was required), so the nth date depends on the (n-1)th ACTUAL FILING DATE without limit. Supply the date the preceding pleading was filed. DO NOT SUPPLY THE RETURN DAY -- the first step alone runs from the return day, that row is NOT seeded, and the return day is a date stated in the writ under Conn. Gen. Stat. Sec. 52-48 (not read), NOT derivable from a service date. NOT SEEDED, though quoted above and real: summary process = THREE days, mortgage foreclosure = FIFTEEN days; both await a domain decision. COUNTING comes from Sec. 63-2 -- last day counted, first day not, 'counted by calendar, not working, days' -- which carries NO short-period exclusion ('intermediate Saturdays' appears zero times in 699 pages), so the three-day variant would need no special handling. DISCLOSED WEAKNESS: Sec. 63-2 sits in the RULES OF APPELLATE PROCEDURE and is the only day-counting provision in the book; if it does not reach trial-court pleadings, the first-day convention here is assumed rather than sourced and would compute LATE. ROLLOVER keys on CLERK'S-OFFICE CLOSURE (Sec. 7-17), NOT on a holiday list, so no calendar is loaded and every computation refuses NOT_PROVISIONED until the Judicial Branch closure schedule is ingested. Sec. 7-17 also deems a document e-received after 5 p.m. filed the next business day -- that moves the FILING, not this date. NO SERVICE EXTENSION EXISTS (searched de-hyphenated, zero hits; Sec. 10-13: 'Service by mail is complete upon mailing'), and none would apply regardless: this period runs from a FILING, not from service.
